data.content:
Henry VI
Henry VI was the King of England during the Wars of the Roses who experienced periods of madness, affecting his reign and leading to civil unrest.<SEP>Henry VI was the King of England during the Wars of the Roses, known for his periods of madness and being dominated by his queen, Margaret of Anjou.

Edward IV
Edward IV was the son of Richard, Duke of York, who became king and united the claims of Lancaster and York through his marriage to Elizabeth of York.

Richard, Duke of York
Richard, Duke of York was a key figure in the Wars of the Roses who started the conflict through his claim to the throne and role as protector of the realm.<SEP>Richard, Duke of York was a key figure in the Wars of the Roses, serving as protector of the realm and leading the Yorkist forces.

Battle of St. Albans
The Battle of St. Albans, fought in 1455, was the first battle of the Wars of the Roses, resulting in a Yorkist victory.

House of Lancaster
The House of Lancaster was one of the two rival factions involved in the Wars of the Roses, represented by the red rose emblem.<SEP>The House of Lancaster is one of the two rival factions in the Wars of the Roses, associated with the red rose and the claim to the English throne.

Battle of Bosworth Field
The Battle of Bosworth Field was the decisive conflict that ended the Wars of the Roses, where Henry Tudor defeated Richard III.<SEP>The Battle of Bosworth Field was the decisive battle in 1485 that ended the Wars of the Roses with the defeat of Richard III.

Second Battle of St. Albans
The Second Battle of St. Albans was a significant conflict in February 1461, where the Lancastrians defeated Warwick’s forces.<SEP>The Second Battle of St. Albans, fought in 1461, was a conflict during the Wars of the Roses where the Lancastrians defeated Warwick.

Lambert Simnel
Lambert Simnel was a pretender to the English throne who represented a Yorkist rising against Henry VII.

Wakefield
Wakefield is a location in England where Richard, Duke of York was killed by Lancastrian forces during the Wars of the Roses.

Henry Tudor
Henry Tudor, later known as Henry VII, was the victor of the Battle of Bosworth Field, which concluded the Wars of the Roses.<SEP>Henry Tudor, later known as Henry VII, was the first monarch of the House of Tudor who ended the Wars of the Roses by defeating Richard III at the Battle of Bosworth Field.

Edward III
Edward III was the King of England whose lineage provided claims to the throne for both the House of Lancaster and the House of York during the Wars of the Roses.<SEP>Edward III was a King of England, the ancestor from whom both the Houses of Lancaster and York claimed their descent.

Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick
Richard Neville, known as the Earl of Warwick, was a leading figure in the Wars of the Roses who supported the Yorkist claim to the throne and had significant military influence.

House of York
The House of York was the rival faction to the House of Lancaster in the Wars of the Roses, symbolized by the white rose emblem.<SEP>The House of York is the rival faction to the House of Lancaster in the Wars of the Roses, identified by the white rose and also claiming the English throne.

Richard III
Richard III was the last king of the House of York, defeated by Henry Tudor at the Battle of Bosworth Field, marking the end of the Wars of the Roses.

Wars of the Roses
The Wars of the Roses were a series of civil wars fought for control of the English throne between the houses of Lancaster and York during the 15th century.<SEP>The Wars of the Roses were a series of dynastic civil wars in England fought between the houses of Lancaster and York for the English throne from 1455 to 1485.

Margaret of Anjou
Margaret of Anjou was the queen consort of Henry VI and played a significant role in the politics of the Wars of the Roses, dominating Henry VI during his madness.<SEP>Margaret of Anjou was the queen of Henry VI, who played a significant role in the conflicts of the Wars of the Roses and led her faction against the Yorkists.

London
London is the capital city of England and the location of the National Portrait Gallery.

National Portrait Gallery
The National Portrait Gallery is an art museum in London known for its collection of portraits, including one of King Edward IV by an unknown artist.

Lancastrians
The Lancastrians were a faction in the Wars of the Roses, opposing the Yorkists and involved in battles for control of the English throne.

York
York, referred to in the context of the text, is a lineage involved in the Wars of the Roses and whose forces faced the Lancastrians.

Warwick
Warwick, known as the Kingmaker, was a significant figure in the Wars of the Roses, supporting the Yorkist claim while opposing the Lancastrians.

Towton
Towton is the site of the bloodiest battle of the Wars of the Roses, where the Yorkists achieved a decisive victory.

Margaret
Margaret is a prominent figure associated with the Lancastrians, opposing Edward IV during the conflict.

Mortimers Cross
Mortimer’s Cross was a battle fought on February 2, 1461, where Edward defeated a Lancastrian force.

Edward
Edward, York’s eldest son, became King Edward IV after military successes against the Lancastrians during the Wars of the Roses.

Duke of York
The Duke of York, referred to in the text, is associated with York’s lineage and was proclaimed King Edward IV after military successes.

Battle of Wakefield
The Battle of Wakefield occurred in December 1460, where York was surprised and killed by the Lancastrians.

Henry VII
Edward IV's daughter, Elizabeth of York, married Henry VII, uniting the claims of both houses at the end of the Wars of the Roses.

King Edward IV
Edward was proclaimed King Edward IV at Westminster, signifying his claim to the throne following military victories.

Henry
Margaret and Henry are linked as a part of the royal family opposing Edward IV in the conflict.<SEP>Henry and Margaret are linked as the royal couple associated with the Lancastrians during the Wars of the Roses.

Western Legal Systems
Western legal systems provide a framework for understanding ownership and possession of property, highlighting the relationship between objects and subjects.

Anglo-American Law
Anglo-American law refers to the legal system that combines English common law with the legal principles of the United States, emphasizing procedural protections of property interests.<SEP>Anglo-American Law generally recognizes multiple possessory rights in land, differing from other legal systems regarding property rights.<SEP>Anglo-American law permits the temporal division of the right of possession, allowing different individuals to hold rights at different times.

United States
The United States features a unique legal framework in property law, especially regarding the constitutional protection of property interests.<SEP>The United States has established a developed legal framework concerning the ownership and regulation of water resources.<SEP>The United States has undergone legal reforms in landlord-tenant law driven by judicial action and subsequent legislation, particularly in the 1960s and 1970s.

Possessory Interests
Possessory interests refer to the rights that individuals or entities have concerning the possession of property, encompassing various classifications and ownership types.

Marital Owners
Marital owners refer to partners in a marriage who jointly hold property rights and interests.

Trusts
Trusts are legal arrangements where property is managed by one party for the benefit of another, involving distinct ownership rights.

Civil Law
Civil law is a legal system based on written codes and statutes, often contrasting with common law systems like Anglo-American law in property definitions and protections.<SEP>Civil Law is characterized by a reluctance to recognize possessory interests in intangible goods compared to Anglo-American Law.<SEP>Civil law is a legal system that also recognizes distinctions between movable and immovable property, similar to Anglo-American law.<SEP>Civil law is a legal system based on written statutes that generally does not recognize divisions of ownership in property.<SEP>Civil law systems typically do not allow for the temporal division of possession rights, focusing instead on the connection between possession and ownership.<SEP>Civil Law refers to a legal system that does not have a direct equivalent to the Anglo-American trust arrangement.

Owner of the House
The owner of the house has legal rights over the property but may not have the right of occupancy if it is held by another person.

Zoning and Planning
Zoning and planning refer to regulatory measures that determine land use and development, impacting property rights and ownership.

House Occupant
The house occupant has exclusive rights of occupancy, which may differ from the ownership rights of the house's owner.

Adverse Possession
Adverse possession allows an individual who occupies land without the owner's permission to eventually claim ownership if certain conditions are met.

Property Law
Property law encompasses the rules governing possessory interests in property, focusing on the objects and subjects of property rights.

Water
Water is recognized as an essential resource within property law, with special regulations governing its ownership and use.<SEP>Water is treated differently from other types of property in the West, with significant legal implications regarding ownership and usage.<SEP>Water is a tangible thing that is removed from private ownership and is generally regarded as belonging to the state or community.

Land
Land includes all terrestrial substances and supports property rights, particularly concerning ownership and use adjacent to water bodies.

Statute of Limitations
The statute of limitations sets a maximum time after an event within which legal proceedings may be initiated, affecting ownership claims.

Peaceable Possessor
The peaceable possessor of land has rights against all claims except those of individuals who can prove a superior right to possession.

Eminent Domain
Eminent domain is the legal principle that allows a government to take private property for public use, providing compensation to the owner.<SEP>Eminent domain is the power of the state to acquire ownership of privately owned assets, usually with compensation to the owner.

Prescription
Prescription is a process in civil law where a possessor acquires title through continuous possession over a certain period.

data.entity_name: Cuius Est Solum Eius Est Usque Ad Coelum Et Usque Ad Inferos
data.content:
Cuius Est Solum Eius Est Usque Ad Coelum Et Usque Ad Inferos
This legal maxim implies that land ownership extends vertically to the sky and down to the center of the earth, influencing ownership interpretations.

Public Regulation of Land Use
Public regulation refers to legal frameworks that govern land use and ownership divisions, potentially affecting property access.

Ownership Types
Ownership types categorize the various forms of property ownership, including single individuals, groups, and corporate owners.

Condominium Ownership
Condominium ownership involves owning a section of property along with shared rights to common areas and utilities.

Vertical Divisions of Ownership
Vertical divisions in ownership refer to the ownership of different rights such as mineral rights and air rights, which can complicate property ownership.

Cooperative Ownership
Cooperative ownership allows multiple owners to share ownership interests in a single property through a corporation structure.

Remainderman
The remainderman holds a future interest in property that begins upon the death of the life tenant, with rights to sue for waste.

Life Estate
Life estate is a legal term describing an interest in property that lasts for the life of a specified individual, after which the interest passes to another entity.<SEP>A life estate grants an individual the right to possess property for their life, with limitations on property use that may affect its value.

Reversion
Reversion refers to the original owner's retained interest in property after granting a life estate to another party.

O-A Deed
The O-A Deed is a legal instrument that provides protection for the party B against party A in property transactions.

Debtor
A Debtor is an individual who owes a debt and may have property rights affected by financial obligations.<SEP>The Debtor is a person who has the right to possession and use of property unless they default on their obligations.

Common-Law Dower
Common-law dower is a legal concept related to the interests of a surviving spouse in the property of the deceased.

Curtesy
Curtesy is a legal right in some jurisdictions that allows a husband to benefit from the property of his deceased wife.

Temporal Divisions
Temporal divisions refer to the legal ability to separate the right of possession from ownership, allowing different individuals to have rights at different times.

Civil-Law System
The civil-law system is a legal tradition that has arrived at similar property results and practices, contrasting with the Anglo-American approach.

Creditor
A Creditor is an individual or institution that lends money and has certain rights over the debtor's property.<SEP>The Creditor is a person or entity that holds a mortgage deed, claiming ownership of the property despite the debtor's rights.

Conditional Sale
Conditional sale is an arrangement where ownership transfers upon fulfillment of certain conditions, typically payments.

Anglo-American System
The Anglo-American system refers to legal practices and principles based on common law traditions.

Chattel Mortgage
Chattel mortgage is a type of security interest allowing the debtor to retain possession of the property while the creditor has rights over it.

Pledge
Pledge is a security agreement where the creditor takes possession of the property, while the debtor retains the right to redeem it.

Pawn
Pawn refers to a transaction where property is given to a creditor as collateral for a loan, with redemption rights for the debtor.

Burglary
Burglary is defined as larceny that involves breaking and entering premises to commit theft.

Robbery
Robbery involves larceny accompanied by the use of force or threats to obtain property from another.

Embezzlement
Embezzlement is the wrongful taking of property by someone who has lawful access to it.

Environmental Law
Environmental law encompasses regulations aimed at protecting community property interests from pollution and environmental harm.

Regulatory Law
Regulatory law is a body of laws designed to govern property use and protect it from adverse effects of regulations.

Property Rights
Property rights are legal rights to own, use, and manage property, which have evolved in both Anglo-American and civil law.<SEP>Property rights refer to the legal entitlements individuals or entities have regarding the use and ownership of property.

Civil Law Criminal Codes
Civil law criminal codes refer to the statutes and legal principles governing theft and related offenses in jurisdictions following civil law traditions.

Administrative Procedure
Administrative procedure allows individuals to compel compliance with regulations through formal processes rather than private lawsuits.

Anglo-American Criminal Codes
Anglo-American criminal codes encompass legal statutes and definitions related to theft and associated crimes within the Anglo-American legal tradition.

Marital Property
Marital property refers to property owned by a couple that may be subject to division during divorce, including community property and separate property.

Community Property
Community property refers to assets acquired by spouses during marriage, shared equally upon dissolution of the marriage or death.<SEP>Community property is the property accumulated during marriage, typically divided equally upon the death of one spouse or divorce.

Separate Property
Separate property consists of property owned individually by one spouse, typically prior to marriage or received as a gift or inheritance.<SEP>Separate property includes assets owned before marriage or received as gifts or inheritance during marriage, which typically remains with the individual owner.

Corporations
Corporations are fictitious legal persons created under incorporation statutes that engage in profit-making activities.

Civil-Law Jurisdictions
Civil-law jurisdictions are legal systems that often have specific rules regarding property rights and ownership, differing from common law.

Public Highways
Public highways are roads owned by the state or community that are generally open for public use under certain conditions.

Common-Law Property Jurisdictions
Common-law property jurisdictions follow a legal system where property division is determined by the judge's discretion during divorce.

State
The state refers to the governing body that can withdraw certain tangible things from private ownership and may own public assets.

Air
Air is regarded by modern Western law as belonging to the state or the community and is not subject to private ownership.

Public Parks
Public parks are recreational areas owned by the state or local government and accessible to the public.

Wild Animals
Wild animals are considered to be tangible things that are typically removed from private ownership by law.

Civil-Law Systems
Civil-law systems encompass legal systems that differ notably in property ownership practices from common law, particularly regarding co-ownership.<SEP>Civil-law systems are legal frameworks that focus on codified statutes and regulations, differing from common-law in their treatment of ownership and possession actions.

American Legal System
The American legal system, comprising common-law and civil-law traditions, is characterized by distinct procedures for property rights and ownership actions.

Triad of Ownership
The triad of ownership refers to the owner's rights to possess, use, and dispose of a thing, commonly referenced in civil-law traditions.

Roman Law
Roman law laid the foundational principles of legal distinction between personal actions and real property actions, influencing later legal systems.

Ejectment Action
The ejectment action is a common-law procedure used to recover possession of land by demonstrating a better right to possession than the defendant.

Trespass
Trespass refers to an unlawful entry onto someone's property, traditionally resulting in personal actions for damages.

Quiet-Title Action
The quiet-title action is an equity procedure aimed at securing judicial recognition of the plaintiff's title to land against opposing claims.

Judicial Declaration
A judicial declaration is a formal judgment regarding the rights or status of parties concerning a legal matter, such as land ownership.

Possessory Actions
Possessory actions are legal proceedings aimed at recovering physical possession of property instead of claims of ownership.

French Revendication
The French revendication is a legal action that allows an individual to recover property through a formal claim, often testing relative ownership rights.

Movable Property Actions
Movable property actions deal with ownership rights and the recovery of personal property rather than real estate.

Fictitious Legal Persons
Fictitious legal persons are organizations such as corporations created under incorporation statutes that can engage in various activities, including profit-making.

Statutory Possessory Action
A statutory possessory action is a legal remedy that allows previous possessors to recover property from those who lack a valid claim of right.

Anglo-American Systems
The Anglo-American systems refer to the legal frameworks derived from English common law and American law, particularly in relation to property ownership and actions.

German Law
German law features a co-ownership model known as Gesamthandeigentum, restricting partitioning of tenancy property among co-owners.<SEP>German law includes various legal actions regarding property rights, closely aligning with foundational principles from Roman law.

Waqf
Waqf is an Islamic legal institution similar to the Anglo-American trust.

Anglo-American Trust
The Anglo-American Trust is a legal arrangement enabling the passage of property interests across generations without probate.

Forcible Entry and Detainer
Forcible entry and detainer refers to legal actions taken to regain possession of property from someone who has unlawfully retained it.

Injunction
An injunction is a court order to prevent an individual from doing something that interferes with the rights of another party, often used in property disputes.

Charitable Trust
The Charitable Trust in Anglo-American law serves specific charitable purposes and has an equivalent in civil law foundations.

Secured Transaction
Secured Transaction involves using property as security for loans or obligations, recognized in both Anglo-American and civil law.

Probate
Probate is a legal process for transferring property following a person’s death, often cumbersome in Anglo-American jurisdictions.

Mortgage
Mortgage is a common law device where property ownership is temporarily transferred to a creditor under certain conditions.

Third Parties
Third Parties are individuals or entities potentially affected by property transactions involving debtors and creditors.

Hypothec
Hypothec is a civil law pledge that allows a debtor to retain possession of property while using it as security for a debt.

Remainder
Remainder is a future interest in property that takes effect after the termination of a prior interest, such as a life estate.

Legal Title
Legal Title refers to formal ownership rights to property, which a debtor may not possess if encumbered by a mortgage.

Contingencies
Contingencies refer to conditions that must be met for certain interests in property or rights to take effect, as described in various legal contexts.

George
George is mentioned as the son of Edith who is to inherit a life estate after his mother’s death and has children who would inherit after him.

Edith
Edith is a person mentioned as the beneficiary of a life estate in the example provided, who will possess the property for her life.

Equity Courts
Equity Courts are judicial entities that protect debtors' rights and ensure fair treatment in property transactions.

Usufruct
Usufruct is a right in civil law that gives a person temporary rights to use and benefit from another's property without owning it.

Fideicommissary Substitutions
Fideicommissary substitutions are legal mechanisms allowing for conditional gifts in civil law, a remnant of ancient Roman law regarding legacies.

Tenancy
Tenancy describes a legal agreement in which one party occupies land or property owned by another party, typically articulated through rental agreements.

Residential Tenancies
Residential tenancies refer to rental agreements that pertain to living accommodations, often subject to specific laws and regulations.<SEP>Residential tenancies pertain to rental agreements for living accommodations, significantly impacted by recent legal changes.

Fee Simple Determinable
Fee simple determinable is a form of fee simple ownership that may automatically terminate when a designated condition occurs, such as failure to use the property for specified purposes.

Commercial Tenancies
Commercial tenancies are legal agreements allowing businesses to lease property for commercial purposes under specific negotiated terms.<SEP>Commercial tenancies are rental agreements for business properties, primarily relying on private negotiations and traditional lease forms.

Landlord-Tenant Relationship
The landlord-tenant relationship pertains to the legal obligations and rights between landlords and tenants regarding property use and possession.

Fee Simple
Fee simple is a type of freehold ownership in property law that provides the most complete form of ownership with the potential for total control of the property, barring certain conditions.

data.entity_name: Fee Simple Subject to a Condition Subsequent
data.content:
Fee Simple Subject to a Condition Subsequent
Fee simple subject to a condition subsequent is a type of fee simple ownership that remains valid unless a specific event occurs that allows the prior owner to reclaim ownership.

Government Grants
Government grants refer to monetary support provided by the government that has become more secure in recent years.

Landlord-Tenant Law
Landlord-tenant law governs the relationship between landlords and tenants, with a trend toward greater security for tenants in the West.

Anglo-American Property Law
Anglo-American property law historically distinguished between interests in land and other types of property, with modern shifts toward more similarity.

Noncitizens
Noncitizens may face restrictions on their property-holding capacity in many jurisdictions, especially in Western countries.

Immovable Property
Immovable property pertains to real estate, such as land and buildings, which has specific legal protections.

Movable Property
Movable property refers to personal possessions that are protected under different legal actions than immovable property.

Children
Children can own property but require parental or guardian consent to deal with it in Western legal systems.

American Indians
American Indians residing on reservations have specific property-holding rules concerning tribal land.

Competent Adult Women
The property-holding capacity and ability to deal with property of competent adult women have been significantly improved in the West.

Property-as-Commodity
Property-as-commodity refers to the view of property as a form of wealth in legal discussions related to ownership and rights.

Property-as-Propriety
Property-as-propriety is the conceptualization of property as the material foundation of a good society, influencing discussions about property rights.

Guardian
A Guardian is appointed to manage the property on behalf of an incompetent individual, authorized to act in their interests.

Incompetent
Incompetent refers to individuals who are unable to manage their property or affairs, necessitating guardianship.

Marital Property Regimes
Marital property regimes are legal frameworks governing the ownership and management of property within marriage, differing across jurisdictions.

Joint Tenancy
Joint tenancy is a form of co-ownership where surviving co-owners inherit the shares of deceased co-owners automatically.

Tenancy in Common
Tenancy in common is a co-ownership format where deceased co-owners' shares pass to their heirs rather than automatically to co-owners.

Cotenancy
Cotenancy refers to a form of shared ownership among multiple owners for property, which may have various legal implications.

French Law
French law provides specific provisions for co-ownership and partition of property among co-owners.

English Common Law
English common law governs partnership property rules and inherited property practices within its legal system.

Tenancy by the Entirety
Tenancy by the entirety is a form of joint property ownership exclusive to married couples, providing survivorship rights.

20th Century
The 20th Century refers to the period from 1901 to 2000, noted for significant legal changes impacting marital property rights.

21st Century
The 21st Century refers to the current period, marked by continuing evolution of laws related to property ownership and marital rights.

Landlord-Tenant Relationships
Landlord-tenant relationships refer to the legal agreements and rights between landlords and tenants, especially in residential and agricultural contexts.

Local Housing Code
Local housing codes set standards for maintaining habitable living conditions in rental properties and are enforced in landlord-tenant relationships.

Agricultural Tenancies
Agricultural tenancies involve rental agreements for agricultural properties, which have also seen extensive legal changes.

data.entity_name: Javins v. First Natl Realty Co.
data.content:
Javins v. First Natl Realty Co.
Javins v. First Nat’l Realty Co. is a landmark court case that established that every residential lease must include a warranty of habitability.

Trust
A trust is a legal arrangement that separates property management from financial benefits, crucial in Anglo-American law.

Trustee
A trustee is an individual or organization appointed to manage property held in trust for the benefit of beneficiaries.

Beneficiary
A beneficiary is an individual who benefits from the trust property, receiving all the advantages while the trustee manages the property.

Spendthrift Trust
A spendthrift trust is a trust that protects a beneficiary’s interest from claims by creditors, permitting secure asset management.

Urban Housing
Urban housing refers to residential housing within city limits, often associated with conditions impacting lower-income residents.

Settlor
A settlor is a person who creates a trust by conveying property to the trustee and stipulating the terms of the trust for beneficiaries.

Legislators
Legislators are individuals elected to make laws, playing a role in enacting changes to landlord-tenant regulations in various jurisdictions.

Deteriorated Housing Conditions
Deteriorated housing conditions refer to the inadequate living situations faced by the urban poor, requiring legal reforms to ensure standards.

Gold
Gold is a mineral that historically was reserved to the crown in England, with significant legal implications for ownership rights.

Lead
Lead is a mineral that historically was reserved to the crown in England, affecting property rights and ownership laws.

Silver
Silver is a mineral previously reserved to the crown in England, shaping ownership laws throughout history.

Copyright
Copyright is the exclusive right to prohibit copying a written piece or artwork, treated as a property right in Western systems.

Patent
A Patent is a government-granted right for exclusive use of an invention, solidified as a key property right in many jurisdictions.

Trademark
A Trademark is a government-granted exclusive right to market products with a distinctive symbol, extending property rights in commerce.

Public Law Program
Public Law Programs involve government grants and protections for property rights, impacting how property is treated legally.

Territorial Waters
Territorial Waters refer to the legal rights and boundaries related to water bodies, which vary substantially from jurisdiction to jurisdiction.

Riparian Right
Riparian Right is a legal concept concerning the rights of landowners whose land borders a river or stream to access and use the water.

Theft
Burglary is classified as a form of theft involving unlawful entry.

Civil-Law Tradition
The triad of ownership is a foundational concept in the civil-law tradition, defining the rights associated with ownership.

Civil Law Foundation
The Charitable Trust has a counterpart in civil law known as the foundation.

Sulfonylureas
Sulfonylureas are a class of oral drugs that stimulate insulin release from beta cells in the pancreas to control blood glucose levels.<SEP>Sulfonylureas are a class of oral diabetes medications that stimulate insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells.

Thiazolidinediones
Thiazolidinediones are a class of oral drugs that reduce insulin resistance and increase glucose transport in muscle and adipose tissues.<SEP>Thiazolidinediones are oral medications utilized to improve insulin sensitivity and control blood glucose levels.

Glimepiride
Glimepiride is another sulfonylurea that helps control blood glucose levels by increasing insulin secretion.

Rosiglitazone
Rosiglitazone is a thiazolidinedione that helps control blood sugar by reducing insulin resistance.

Exenatide
Exenatide is an injectable antihyperglycemic drug that mimics incretin hormones to stimulate insulin release.

Pramlintide
Pramlintide is an injectable hormone that regulates blood glucose by slowing food absorption and inhibiting glucagon.

Diabetes
Diabetes is a chronic condition affecting glucose regulation and metabolism, treated with various oral and injectable drugs.

Pioglitazone
Pioglitazone is another thiazolidinedione that improves insulin sensitivity in muscle and adipose cells.

Biguanides
Biguanides are a class of oral drugs, primarily metformin, that decrease glucose production in the liver and increase insulin action on tissues.<SEP>Biguanides are another class of oral drugs used for blood glucose control in diabetes.

Glipizide
Glipizide is a specific sulfonylurea used to lower blood glucose levels by stimulating insulin release.

Lactic Acid
Lactic acid is a substance that can accumulate in blood and tissues as a potentially fatal side effect of metformin.

Metformin
Metformin is the primary biguanide that decreases liver glucose production and enhances insulin action on tissues.

Sitagliptin
Sitagliptin is a drug that inhibits DPP-4, increasing levels of incretins to enhance glucose control.

Semaglutide
Semaglutide mimics glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) to help regulate glucose and induce satiety.

Edema
Edema is a condition characterized by fluid accumulation in tissues, which can be caused by thiazolidinediones.

Diabetes Mellitus
Diabetes Mellitus is a chronic condition characterized by high blood sugar levels, requiring monitoring and management, usually through insulin therapies and diet control.

Insulin Therapies
Insulin therapies are treatments aimed at managing diabetes by administering insulin to control blood glucose levels, often involving various types of insulin formulations.

Beef Insulin
Beef insulin is a form of insulin derived from cattle's pancreatic extracts, previously used for diabetes treatment but discontinued in the United States.

Hypoglycemia
Hypoglycemia is a condition characterized by abnormally low blood glucose levels, often due to certain medications.

Pork Insulin
Pork insulin is a form of insulin derived from pigs' pancreatic extracts, previously used for diabetes treatment but discontinued in favor of human insulin.

Rapid-Acting Insulin
Rapid-acting insulin is a type of insulin that lowers blood glucose levels quickly, typically administered before meals, and includes an inhalable form introduced in 2014.

Glucometer
A glucometer is a device used by diabetics to monitor their blood glucose levels regularly.

Long-Acting Insulin
Long-acting insulin is designed to provide a prolonged effect, managing blood glucose levels for up to 24 hours after administration.

Beta Cell Transplantation
Beta cell transplantation involves replacing damaged or non-functioning insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas.

Human Insulin
Human insulin is a synthetic form of insulin produced using recombinant DNA technology, used in modern diabetes treatment and available in various formulations.

Pancreas Transplantation
Pancreas transplantation is a surgical method used to treat patients with type 1 diabetes by replacing the diseased pancreas.

Insulin Pump
An insulin pump is a medical device that delivers insulin continuously to help manage blood glucose levels in diabetes patients.
